title: Hungary
content: Hungary's industrial sector experienced a significant contraction of 7.3% in August 2025 compared to the same month in the previous year, according to data released on October 14, 2025. This marks a sharp deterioration from the prior month's 1.0% decline. The downturn reflects mounting economic pressures, potentially driven by global supply chain disruptions, fluctuating demand, or domestic economic policies affecting productivity. The contraction signals potential headwinds for broader economic expansion, particularly in manufacturing and exports. Economists and policymakers are expected to analyze the data to develop strategies to stabilize or revive industrial activity. The coming months will be closely monitored to determine whether the trend reverses or continues, with implications for Hungary's overall economic outlook.

title: Surge in Hungary
content: Hungary's retail sales increased by 2.4% year-over-year in August 2025, up from 1.7% in July 2025, according to data updated on October 6, 2025. This growth reflects a strengthening in consumer confidence and suggests potential resilience in Hungary's economic framework amid global fluctuations. The improvement indicates a positive trend in consumer spending and may signal stabilization or even flourishing market conditions. Analysts and stakeholders are expected to monitor future sales data to assess continued growth potential and overall economic health in Hungary's retail sector.

title: Ungarn setzen andere Prioritäten - Budapester Zeitung
content: A Eurobarometer survey published by the Budapester Zeitung on 4 September 2025 shows that EU citizens and Hungarians prioritize different policy areas. In the EU‑27, respondents named defence and security as the top priority (37 % of mentions), followed by competitiveness (32 %) and energy sovereignty (27 %). In Hungary, competitiveness received the highest share (36 %), narrowly ahead of food safety and agriculture (35 %), with defence and energy sovereignty tied at 29 % each. Culture, EU enlargement and the euro were the least mentioned topics in both groups. The survey also asked respondents which issues the European Parliament should address. 41 % of EU citizens and 46 % of Hungarians said the Parliament should focus on inflation, rising prices and living costs. Hungarians additionally wanted support for the economy (37 %) and health care (33 %). Topics receiving the least attention included equality, inclusion, diversity, development aid, digitalisation and consumer protection. Regarding the EU’s benefits, 37 % of EU‑27 respondents cited the preservation of peace, whereas only 24 % of Hungarians did. Hungarians ranked better employment opportunities as the most important benefit (41 %) and valued the EU’s contribution to economic growth (33 %). The survey found that two‑thirds of younger EU citizens (15‑40 years) support EU enlargement, with the greatest perceived benefits in common security and defence policy, economic competitiveness and the EU’s global role. However, more than two‑thirds of respondents expressed dissatisfaction with the information available on the enlargement process. Regional attitudes varied: 91 % of Albanians, 74 % of Georgians, 68 % of Ukrainians and 49 % of Russians support EU membership, while only 33 % of Serbians do.

title: Ungarischer Nationalfeiertag lässt Kassen im Burgenland klingeln
content: The Hungarian National Day on August 20th is expected to attract many customers from Hungary to the Burgenland region. According to a study by 'Gut & Co - Gumpinger Test & Consulting', the influx of purchasing power from Hungary amounts to around 178 million euros per year. The eastern neighbors have become indispensable not only as workers but also as consumers for the Burgenland economy, despite the fact that the Hungarian economy is also experiencing a slowdown. After a decline, the Hungarian economy is expected to grow slightly in 2024. As a result, the Burgenland trade is well-prepared and full of hope for the influx of customers.

title: Überraschungen hier wie da - Budapester Zeitung
content: The Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) released its first estimate for the second quarter of 2025, showing that the gross domestic product (GDP) grew 0,2 % year‑on‑year, up from 0,4 % in the previous quarter – a slight rebound after a stagnant first half of the year. Construction was the biggest surprise, adding 4,3 % to output, while the ITK sector grew 6,3 % and the culture‑and‑leisure industry 6,5 %. Tourism, education, finance and trade also posted gains of 3,2 %, 2,9 %, 2,2 % and 1,8 % respectively. Industry fell 3,3 % and manufacturing declined 4,4 %. Agriculture recorded a sharp 11,4 % drop, though early harvest data suggest a possible rebound later in the year. On the use side, private consumption rose 4,5 %, domestic consumption 5,3 %, but investment fell 7,0 %. Exports stagnated, imports grew 4,0 %, and the net foreign trade surplus of 1 200 billion Forint narrowed GDP by 3,4 percentage points. As KSH noted, 'BIP im II. Quartal auf Jahresebene – saisonal und nach Kalendertagen bereinigt – um 0,2 %'. The report also highlighted that 'BIP im I. Halbjahr stagnierte die Wirtschaft unterm Strich.'

title: Hungary Retail Sales Growth Eases In July
content: According to preliminary figures from the Hungarian Central Statistical Office, retail sales in Hungary rose 1.7 percent year‑over‑year in July, a slowdown from the 3.0 percent increase recorded in June.  Sales volumes grew 3.4 percent in non‑specialised food and beverage shops, while specialised food, beverage and tobacco stores saw a 1.2 percent decline.  Automotive fuel sales fell 0.4 percent.  Mail‑order and internet sales, which account for 8.1 percent of total retail sales, increased 6.8 percent year‑over‑year.  On a monthly basis, seasonally and working‑day‑adjusted retail sales fell 0.5 percent in July.

title: Hungarian Budget Under Pressure
content: Hungary's monthly budget deficit reached HUF 303.2 billion in September 2025, contributing to a year-to-date general government cash-flow deficit of HUF 3.33 trillion—70% of the full-year 2025 target. The 12-month rolling deficit rose to HUF 4.9 trillion, the highest level since March 2024, marking a sustained deterioration. This deterioration followed the end of one-off revenues such as dividend income, which had previously masked fiscal weakness. The deficit-to-GDP ratio is projected to reach 4.6% in 2025 and 4.5% in 2026, exceeding the official target of 4.1%. The main drivers of the shortfall are insufficient corporate-related revenues. Despite this, ING maintains that the government can achieve its deficit target with effort, noting that upcoming fiscal measures—such as tax changes for mothers, military bonuses, pensioner lump sums, wage settlements, and lending programs—total 2.0–2.5% of GDP, with only a small portion unbudgeted and impacting 2026, unlike the 3.3% of GDP in 2021/22. The upcoming general election in spring 2026 raises concerns about potential pre-election spending, though the government has taken a more conservative approach. Economic risks, particularly weak third-quarter performance and political tensions, could worsen the deficit further. However, the outlook remains that the deficit will fall below last year’s 5.0% of GDP and continue to decline modestly in 2026. A stronger Hungarian forint (HUF) could limit the rise in debt-to-GDP ratio, though this remains uncertain.
